topics.title: The UK government, the law and your role

questions.text: Which of these is a fundamental principle of British life?
choices: Obedience to religious law above national law
questions.explanation: Fundamental principles include democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of different faiths, and participation in community life.

questions.text: Which of these is a responsibility of people living in the UK?
questions.explanation: Residents should respect and obey the law, respect the rights of others, treat others fairly, look after themselves and their family, and look after the area they live in.

questions.text: Which of these is a freedom people in the UK have?
questions.explanation: In return, the UK offers freedom of belief and religion, freedom of speech, freedom from unfair discrimination, a right to a fair trial and a right to join in the election of a government.

questions.text: What are the four countries of the United Kingdom?
choices: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
England, Scotland, Wales and the Isle of Man
England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland
questions.explanation: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Great Britain is England, Scotland and Wales.

questions.text: Are the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man part of the UK?
choices: Yes, they are part of England
Yes, they are part of Scotland
They are independent countries outside the Commonwealth
No, they are Crown dependencies with their own governments
questions.explanation: The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are closely linked to the UK but are not part of it.

questions.text: What is the capital of the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: London is the capital of the UK. Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland, Cardiff of Wales and Belfast of Northern Ireland.

questions.text: What is the capital of Wales?
questions.explanation: Cardiff is the capital of Wales.

questions.text: What is the capital of Northern Ireland?
questions.explanation: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland. Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland.

questions.text: Who invaded Britain in 55 BC but did not stay?
questions.explanation: Julius Caesar led a Roman invasion in 55 BC; the Romans returned under Emperor Claudius in AD 43 and stayed for about 400 years.

questions.text: Who built a wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts?
questions.explanation: Hadrian's Wall was built by the Romans; parts of it can still be seen today.

questions.text: In which year did the Normans, led by William, Duke of Normandy, defeat the English at the Battle of Hastings?
questions.explanation: William defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings in 1066; the battle is shown in the Bayeux Tapestry.

questions.text: What tapestry commemorates the Battle of Hastings?
questions.explanation: The Bayeux Tapestry, which can still be seen in France, shows the Norman conquest.

questions.text: What was the Domesday Book?
choices: A list of soldiers at Hastings
A book of laws written by King Alfred
A record of towns, villages, people and livestock in England made by William the Conqueror
questions.explanation: The Domesday Book gives a picture of society in England just after the Norman Conquest.

questions.text: What did the Magna Carta of 1215 establish?
choices: That the Church of England was the official church
That even the king was subject to the law
questions.explanation: King John was forced to agree to the Magna Carta, which limited the power of the monarch.

questions.text: Which battle in 1415 is remembered for the victory of King Henry V over the French?
questions.explanation: Henry V's army won the Battle of Agincourt during the Hundred Years War.

questions.text: Which Scottish victory in 1314 kept Scotland unconquered by the English?
questions.explanation: Robert the Bruce defeated the English at Bannockburn in 1314.

questions.text: What were the Wars of the Roses?
choices: A civil war between the House of Lancaster and the House of York
A religious war about the Church of England
A war between Scotland and Wales
A war between England and France
questions.explanation: The Wars of the Roses ended in 1485 with Henry Tudor's victory at Bosworth Field; he became Henry VII.

questions.text: Why did Henry VIII establish the Church of England?
choices: To end the Wars of the Roses
Because the Pope refused to allow him to divorce his first wife
questions.explanation: Henry VIII broke away from the Roman Catholic Church so that he could divorce Catherine of Aragon.

questions.text: How many times did Henry VIII marry?
questions.explanation: Henry VIII married six times: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard and Catherine Parr.

questions.text: In which year was the Spanish Armada defeated?
questions.explanation: Queen Elizabeth I's navy defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588.

questions.text: Who is considered one of the greatest playwrights in the English language, writing plays such as "Romeo and Juliet"?
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote many plays and poems still performed and studied today.

questions.text: What was the Gunpowder Plot of 1605?
choices: A failed plan to blow up the Houses of Parliament
questions.explanation: Guy Fawkes and other Catholics plotted to kill King James I; it is remembered on Bonfire Night, 5 November.

questions.text: What happened in 1666?
choices: The defeat of the Spanish Armada
questions.explanation: The Great Fire of London destroyed much of the city; Sir Christopher Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral.

questions.text: Who designed the new St Paul's Cathedral after the Great Fire of London?
questions.explanation: Sir Christopher Wren rebuilt many churches in London, including St Paul's Cathedral.

questions.text: Who led the Parliamentary army in the English Civil War and later ruled as Lord Protector?
questions.explanation: After Charles I was executed in 1649, England became a republic and Cromwell became Lord Protector.

questions.text: What was the Glorious Revolution of 1688?
choices: The peaceful replacement of James II by William of Orange and Mary
The union of England and Ireland
questions.explanation: William and Mary took the throne without fighting in England; the Bill of Rights of 1689 followed.

questions.text: Who is generally regarded as the first Prime Minister of Britain?
questions.explanation: Sir Robert Walpole was Prime Minister from 1721 to 1742.

questions.text: In which year did the Act of Union create the Kingdom of Great Britain, uniting England, Wales and Scotland?
questions.explanation: The Act of Union of 1707 united Scotland with England and Wales.

questions.text: Which admiral defeated the French and Spanish fleets at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
questions.explanation: Nelson was killed in the battle; Nelson's Column stands in Trafalgar Square, London.

questions.text: Who defeated Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
questions.explanation: The Duke of Wellington, later Prime Minister, defeated Napoleon at Waterloo.

questions.text: Which period of rapid development in industry began in Britain in the 18th century?
questions.explanation: Britain was the first country to industrialise on a large scale, with new machines, coal, iron and railways.

questions.text: Who was a famous engineer who built tunnels, bridges, railway lines and ships, such as the Great Western Railway?
questions.explanation: Brunel built the Great Western Railway and the Clifton Suspension Bridge design among many works.

questions.text: Who was Queen of the UK for 63 years from 1837, a period of great industrial and imperial expansion?
questions.explanation: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901; the period is called the Victorian age.

questions.text: Who campaigned for women's right to vote and founded the Women's Franchise League?
questions.explanation: Emmeline Pankhurst led the suffragettes, who campaigned for women's votes.

questions.text: In which year did women over 21 get the right to vote on the same terms as men?
questions.explanation: In 1918 women over 30 gained the vote; in 1928 women got the vote at 21, the same as men.

questions.text: Who is known as the founder of modern nursing, having cared for soldiers in the Crimean War?
questions.explanation: Florence Nightingale established the Nightingale Training School for nurses at St Thomas' Hospital in 1860.

questions.text: Who was the British Prime Minister during most of the Second World War?
questions.explanation: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in 1940 and led Britain to victory; he is famous for his speeches.

questions.text: Which battle in 1940 saw the RAF defeat the German air force over Britain?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Britain was fought in the skies in the summer of 1940.

questions.text: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
questions.explanation: Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic.

questions.text: When was the National Health Service (NHS) established?
questions.explanation: The NHS was established in 1948 to provide free healthcare at the point of use.

questions.text: Who was the first woman Prime Minister of the UK?
questions.explanation: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990.

questions.text: Who invented the World Wide Web?
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web; it was first used successfully in 1990.

questions.text: What is the patron saint of England, and when is his day?
questions.explanation: The patron saints are St George (England, 23 April), St Andrew (Scotland, 30 November), St David (Wales, 1 March) and St Patrick (Northern Ireland, 17 March).

questions.text: Who is the patron saint of Scotland?
questions.explanation: St Andrew's Day is 30 November.

questions.text: Who is the patron saint of Wales?
questions.explanation: St David's Day is 1 March.

questions.text: When is Christmas Day celebrated?
questions.explanation: Christmas Day, 25 December, celebrates the birth of Jesus Christ. Boxing Day is 26 December.

questions.text: What is Bonfire Night (5 November) a celebration of?
choices: The end of the Second World War
The defeat of the Spanish Armada
The failure of the Gunpowder Plot in 1605
questions.explanation: People let off fireworks and light bonfires to mark the failed plot to blow up Parliament.

questions.text: What is remembered on Remembrance Day, 11 November?
choices: The union of England and Scotland
Those who died fighting for the UK and its allies
questions.explanation: Remembrance Day marks the end of the First World War in 1918; people wear poppies and hold a two-minute silence.

questions.text: What is the national flag of the UK called?
questions.explanation: The Union Flag combines the crosses of St George, St Andrew and St Patrick.

questions.text: Which country's flag is not represented on the Union Flag?
questions.explanation: Wales is not represented because it was united with England when the first Union Flag was created in 1606; the Welsh flag shows a red dragon.

questions.text: What does the Welsh national flag show?
questions.explanation: The Welsh flag shows a red dragon on a white and green background.

questions.text: Which famous horse race is held at Aintree near Liverpool?
questions.explanation: The Grand National is a famous steeplechase at Aintree.

questions.text: Which tennis championship is held every year in London?
questions.explanation: Wimbledon, the oldest tennis tournament in the world, is held at the All England Club.

questions.text: In which city were the Olympic Games held in 2012?
questions.explanation: London hosted the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2012.

questions.text: Which sport originated in England and is played in summer, with matches that can last up to five days?
questions.explanation: Cricket originated in England and is popular in many Commonwealth countries.

questions.text: Which of these is a traditional food associated with Scotland?
questions.explanation: Haggis is a traditional Scottish dish; roast beef and Yorkshire pudding are English, Welsh cakes Welsh and the Ulster fry from Northern Ireland.

questions.text: Who wrote the novels "Oliver Twist" and "Great Expectations"?
questions.explanation: Charles Dickens is one of the most famous novelists of the Victorian period.

questions.text: Who wrote "Pride and Prejudice"?
questions.explanation: Jane Austen (1775–1817) wrote novels about marriage and family relationships.

questions.text: Which Scottish poet wrote "Auld Lang Syne"?
questions.explanation: Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet; "Auld Lang Syne" is sung at New Year.

questions.text: What is the Cenotaph?
choices: The home of the Prime Minister
A war memorial in Whitehall, London
questions.explanation: The Cenotaph in Whitehall is the focus of the Remembrance Sunday service.

questions.text: What is the Eden Project?
choices: A museum of science in London
Large greenhouses in Cornwall holding plants from around the world
questions.explanation: The Eden Project in Cornwall has giant greenhouses with plants from many climates.

questions.text: Which of these is a famous landmark in Scotland?
questions.explanation: Edinburgh Castle dominates the skyline of Scotland's capital. The Giant's Causeway is in Northern Ireland.

questions.text: What type of government does the UK have?
choices: A parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarchy
questions.explanation: The monarch is Head of State but does not rule; Parliament makes the laws.

questions.text: What are the two Houses of Parliament?
choices: The House of Commons and the Senate
The House of Commons and the House of Lords
The House of Lords and the Cabinet
The Senate and the House of Representatives
questions.explanation: The House of Commons is elected; members of the House of Lords are not elected.

questions.text: Who is the Head of State of the UK?
questions.explanation: The UK is a constitutional monarchy: the King is Head of State and has a largely ceremonial role.

questions.text: Who is the head of the government in the UK?
choices: The Speaker of the House of Commons
questions.explanation: The Prime Minister leads the government and usually lives at 10 Downing Street.

questions.text: Where does the Prime Minister usually live?
questions.explanation: 10 Downing Street, off Whitehall in London, is the Prime Minister's official residence. The Chancellor of the Exchequer uses No. 11.

questions.text: What is the role of the Speaker of the House of Commons?
choices: To keep order during debates and make sure rules are followed
questions.explanation: The Speaker is chosen by MPs, is neutral, and chairs debates in the House of Commons.

questions.text: How often must a general election be held in the UK?
questions.explanation: General elections are held at least every five years.

questions.text: What is the minimum voting age in UK general elections?
questions.explanation: People aged 18 or over can vote in UK Parliament elections if they are British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizens and registered.

questions.text: Who can vote in UK general elections?
choices: Only people born in the UK
Registered UK, Irish and qualifying Commonwealth citizens aged 18 or over
questions.explanation: Citizens of other EU countries cannot vote in UK Parliament elections.

questions.text: What is the official church of England?
questions.explanation: The Church of England (Anglican) is the state church in England; the monarch is its Supreme Governor.

questions.text: Which countries in the UK have their own devolved parliaments or assemblies?
questions.explanation: The Scottish Parliament, the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) and the Northern Ireland Assembly make laws on certain matters.

questions.text: Where does the Scottish Parliament sit?
questions.explanation: The Scottish Parliament meets at Holyrood in Edinburgh. The Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont.

questions.text: Which court is the highest court of appeal in the UK for civil cases?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court is the final court of appeal for civil cases in the UK and criminal cases in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

questions.text: In England and Wales, which court deals with most minor criminal cases?
questions.explanation: Minor criminal offences are dealt with in magistrates' courts; serious offences go to the Crown Court with a jury.

questions.text: What number do you call in an emergency in the UK?
questions.explanation: 999 or 112 is for emergencies; 111 is the NHS non-emergency number and 101 the police non-emergency number.

questions.text: Which international organisation did the UK help to found after the Second World War to keep peace between nations?
questions.explanation: The UK is one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

questions.text: What is the Commonwealth?
choices: An association of countries, most of which were once part of the British Empire
questions.explanation: The monarch is head of the Commonwealth; membership is voluntary.
